subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: defining what AI may and may not do [Thinking]
passage:
'Let's decide before someone decides for us,' said Vijay, uncapping a marker. 'What can we use AI tools for?'
'Drafting test cases,' said Parul. 'Summarising public documents.'
'Yes. Also a first draft of release notes. What goes on the no side?'
'Anything with customer data.'
'Right. And passwords, keys, anything from the private repo pasted into a public tool. If I wouldn't pin it on a notice board outside, it doesn't go in.'
'What about code it writes?'
'Fine as a draft, but a person reads it before it merges. It can sound sure and be wrong.'
Parul wrote both lists on the whiteboard. 'It's clearer with a line down the middle,' she said. Vijay drew it, and they photographed the board for the group chat.

qa.q: Which two uses did Parul name as allowed?
qa.a: Parul named drafting test cases and summarising public documents.

qa.q: What does Vijay seem worried about at the start?
qa.a: Vijay seems worried that people will start using the tools in risky ways on their own, so Vijay wants a clear line agreed first.

qa.q: What other approach could help the rules stick?
qa.a: Vijay could put them on a short shared page and revisit it in a month, since tools and habits change quickly.

qa.q: How might Parul see the line down the middle?
qa.a: Parul finds it clearer, saying so, because two lists become a boundary the team can point to.

grounding: Shows a team lead listing the uses of AI tools that are allowed and those that are not, including keeping customer data and secrets out of public tools.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: defining what AI may and may not do [Thinking]
passage:
I'm Chinmay, and I became the person who wrote 'the AI list' by accident. Baljeet, one of my developers, asked on a Monday, 'Can I paste the customer's error log into that chatbot to understand it?' I realised I didn't have an answer.
So that evening I sat and thought it through. What does the tool do well for us? Drafting unit tests. Summarising public documentation. Explaining an unfamiliar error message, if I strip out anything private. What could hurt us? Customer data leaving our systems. Passwords or keys in a prompt. Code we can't explain going live.
Next morning I put two columns on the team board. Allowed: drafting tests, summarising public docs, explaining generic errors. Not allowed: customer data, secrets, anything we paste without reading. Baljeet read it and said, 'So I strip the log first.' Exactly.

qa.q: What did Baljeet ask on Monday?
qa.a: Whether the customer's error log could be pasted into that chatbot to understand it.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel on realising there was no answer?
qa.a: Chinmay felt caught off guard and a little uneasy, which led to thinking it through that evening.

qa.q: What else could Chinmay add to the two columns?
qa.a: Chinmay could add a short line on who to ask in a grey case, so developers don't have to guess.

qa.q: How does the board look to Baljeet?
qa.a: Baljeet gets a clear answer and a simple rule, strip the log first, instead of worrying about getting it wrong.

grounding: It shows a team lead listing allowed AI uses, such as drafting tests and summarising public documents, and forbidden ones, such as pasting customer data or secrets.

subtopic: Using AI tools inside a team
subtype: Approach: defining what AI may and may not do [Thinking]
passage:
Note to file, engineering managers' meeting, 3 May.
Aadhya, who leads the mobile team, presented how her team decided what AI tools may and may not do. I want it on record because it was the clearest thinking in the room.
She had started from risks, not from features. Her list of allowed uses: drafting test cases, summarising public API documentation, suggesting names and comments. Her list of forbidden uses: pasting customer records, pasting API keys or passwords, using any output that no human has read. She explained each line with a real near miss from her team.
Two managers wanted to copy it at once. I have asked Aadhya to share it with all teams by Friday and to note where each team might need to differ.
Tejas

qa.q: What might Aadhya have felt when two managers wanted to copy the list?
qa.a: Aadhya probably felt proud and encouraged that the careful thinking was useful beyond the mobile team.

qa.q: Why was explaining each line with a real near miss effective?
qa.a: Real examples made the rules concrete and believable, so other managers could see why each limit exists.

qa.q: How might other teams be affected by Tejas's request?
qa.a: They get a tested starting list by Friday, with room to note where their work differs.

grounding: It shows a manager's note on a team lead who lists allowed AI uses like drafting tests and forbidden ones like pasting customer data or secrets.
